title: Λύκος ⟨τετρωμένος⟩ καὶ πρόβατον
titleEn: The Wounded Wolf and the Sheep
part: The Wounded Wolf and the Sheep (Chambry 231)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 231. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος ὑπὸ κυνῶν δηχθεὶς καὶ κακῶς διατεθεὶς ἐβέβλητο τροφὴν ἑαυτῷ περιποιεῖσθαι μὴ δυνάμενος· καὶ δὴ θεασάμενος πρόβατον, τούτου ἐδεήθη ποτὸν αὐτῷ ὀρέξαι ἐκ τοῦ παραρρέοντος ποταμοῦ· « Ἐὰν γὰρ σύ μοι ποτὸν δῷς, ἐγὼ τὴν τροφὴν ἐμαυτῷ εὑρήσω. »
sentences.tr: Lykos hypo kynōn dēchtheis kai kakōs diatetheis ebeblēto trophēn heautōi peripoieisthai mē dynamenos· kai dē theasamenos probaton, toutou edeēthē poton autōi orexai ek tou pararreontos potamou· « Ean gar sy moi poton dōis, egō tēn trophēn emautōi heurēsō. »
sentences.l: A wolf, bitten by dogs and put in a bad way, lay flung down, not being able to procure food for himself; and indeed, having caught sight of a sheep, he begged of it to hold out a drink to him from the river flowing past: « For if you give me a drink, I shall find the food for myself. »
sentences.i: A wolf, bitten by dogs and in a bad way, lay there unable to get himself any food; and catching sight of a sheep, he begged it to bring him a drink from the river running by: « If you give me a drink, I shall find my own food. »
sentences.n: ἐβέβλητο is the pluperfect passive of βάλλω, used of a body that has been laid low and stays down — 'he lay flung there'. δέομαι takes the genitive of the person asked (τούτου) and an infinitive of the thing asked. διατίθημι with an adverb means to put someone in a state: κακῶς διατεθείς, 'put in a bad way'. The wolf's request is careful: he asks only for water, and lets the sheep infer that the food will come from somewhere else.

sentences.t: Τὸ δὲ ὑποτυχὸν ἔφη· « Ἐὰν ποτόν σοι ἐπιδώσω ἐγώ, σὺ καὶ τροφῇ μοι χρήσῃ. »
sentences.tr: To de hypotychon ephē· « Ean poton soi epidōsō egō, sy kai trophēi moi chrēsēi. »
sentences.l: And it, taking-up-the-word, said: « If I give you a drink, you will use me for food as well. »
sentences.i: But the sheep answered: « If I hand you the drink, you will make use of me for food as well. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχόν is the house idiom for breaking in with a reply, not for any physical seizing; it is neuter here because πρόβατον is neuter. χράομαι takes the dative of what is used, and τροφῇ μοι sets two datives side by side — 'use me as your food'.

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα κακοῦργον δι’ ὑποκρίσεως ἐνεδρεύοντα ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros andra kakourgon di’ hypokriseōs enedreuonta ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against a criminal man, lying in wait by means of pretence, the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story is well aimed at the criminal who sets his ambush behind a pretence.
sentences.n: ὑπόκρισις is the actor's art, the playing of a part, and so a feigned appearance; the wolf's show of asking for water only is exactly that.
